title: Ex 8.18 · Product distributes over difference
prompt: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be any sets. Prove that $A \times (B - C) = (A \times B) - (A \times C)$. The elements of these sets are ordered pairs, so follow a pair $(x, y)$.
answer_format: A chain of lines, each a set (like A × (B ∪ C)) or a statement about an ordered pair (x, y) (like x ∈ A and y ∈ B, or (x, y) ∈ A × B). Each line must have exactly the same elements as the line before; start from the left side and end at the right side.
hints: (x, y) ∈ A × (B − C) means x ∈ A and y ∈ B and y ∉ C.
On the right, (x, y) ∉ A × C means not (x ∈ A and y ∈ C), which by De Morgan's law is x ∉ A or y ∉ C.
When x ∈ A is true, 'x ∉ A or y ∉ C' says the same thing as y ∉ C. So x ∈ A and y ∈ B and y ∉ C matches (x ∈ A and y ∈ B) and (x ∉ A or y ∉ C).
solution: Let $(x, y)$ be any ordered pair. Then $(x, y) \in A \times (B - C)$ means $x \in A \land (y \in B \land y \notin C)$.

Whenever $x \in A$ is true, $y 
otin C$ is equivalent to $x 
otin A \lor y 
otin C$. So the statement is $(x \in A \land y \in B) \land (x 
otin A \lor y 
otin C)$.
By De Morgan's law the second part is $\sim(x \in A \land y \in C)$, which says $(x, y) \notin A \times C$; the first part says $(x, y) \in A \times B$.
So $(x, y) \in (A \times B) - (A \times C)$. Every step was an equivalence, so $A \times (B - C) = (A \times B) - (A \times C)$. $\blacksquare$

reference.note: This exact exercise, restated in ProofLab's words. Uses Section 8.3 (proving A = B), the Cartesian product (Section 1.2) and the logic laws of Section 2.6.

steps.content: x ∈ A and (y ∈ B and y ∉ C)
(x ∈ A and y ∈ B) and (x ∉ A or y ∉ C)
(x ∈ A and y ∈ B) and not (x ∈ A and y ∈ C)
(x, y) ∈ A × B and (x, y) ∉ A × C
x ∈ A and (y ∈ B and y ∉ C)
(x ∈ A and y ∈ B) and (x ∉ A and y ∉ C)
